title: City-Level Effectiveness of the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) in India
summary: Did India's National Clean Air Programme lower fine-particle pollution in its target cities? Satellite data from 1998 to 2023 and a synthetic difference-in-differences design say it has not, so far.
opening: Did India's clean air programme cut pollution? Not so far.
abstract: The effectiveness of India’s National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) is evaluated using high-resolution satellite data (1998–2023). A standard Difference-in-Differences (DiD) baseline is first employed, but it is found to be unsuitable due to violations of parallel trend assumptions. Consequently, a Synthetic Difference-in-Differences (SDiD) estimator is utilised to rigorously isolate policy impacts. It is indicated by the results that aggregate urban pollution trajectories were not altered by the NCAP between 2019 and 2023.

No improvement relative to synthetic counterfactuals is shown in national estimates, though significant regional heterogeneity is observed: deterioration relative to the counterfactual is recorded in the Arid West, while modest reductions are exhibited in the North-East & East. Crucially, no correlation between fund utilisation and air quality outcomes is found via meta-regression, suggesting that effectiveness has not been driven by spending. The insufficiency of the NCAP’s design — relying on non-binding, city-specific mechanical interventions — is implied by these widespread null results. A shift from city-centric plans to enforceable, source-specific interventions coordinated across transboundary airsheds is required to effectively combat India’s pollution.

question.lead: Has India's National Clean Air Programme made the air cleaner in the cities it targets?
question.text: The programme began in January 2019. It named 131 “non-attainment” cities, set out to cut particulate pollution by 20–30% by 2024 (later 40% by 2026), and has been allocated about US$ 1.6 billion. The thesis asks whether fine-particle pollution (PM2.5) in those cities fell below what it would have been without the programme.

figure.caption: Annual mean PM2.5 in the NCAP cities (blue) and in their synthetic counterpart (grey), 1998–2023. The dashed line marks the start of the programme in 2019. For two decades before that the two lines move together; after it the NCAP cities sit slightly above their counterpart, not below it.

finding.lead: No detectable reduction in PM2.5 between 2019 and 2023.
points: The national estimate for 2019–2023 (standard error 0.25). Pollution in NCAP cities came out slightly above their counterfactual, not below it.

What a standard difference-in-differences model estimates, one figure for each of the two control groups. NCAP cities were already on a different path before 2019, and once that is accounted for the estimate shrinks.
Regions differ. In the Arid West pollution came out above its counterfactual; in the North-East & East it came out a little below.
How much of the difference between cities' results is explained by the share of its allocated funds each city spent. Spending more did not go with cleaner air.

The NCAP cities are measured through the sub-district or district they lie in, so the areas studied are less precise than intended. The official data portal was unavailable for much of the research period, and collecting the data by hand did not fit the time available.
Some fine-grained controls are missing, such as fuel use or industrial density at sub-district level, which could explain more of the variation in pollution.
In the Indo-Gangetic Plain the placebo tests are unstable. Pollution there is so strongly correlated across neighbouring areas that a clean comparison group is hard to build, even with this method.
The thesis covers only the programme's first five years, and the programme as a whole. A longer period, other pollutants and the individual measures are left for later work.
